# RFC 9457 Specification

Covers Dimension 1: What RFC 9457 specifies and how it supersedes RFC 7807.

See [citations.md](../citations.md) for full source details.

## Standard Members

RFC 9457 defines five standard members. All are optional [1]:

| Member | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `type` | URI reference | Problem type identifier; defaults to `about:blank` [1] |
| `status` | integer (100-599) | HTTP status code; advisory only [1] |
| `title` | string | Human-readable summary; SHOULD NOT change between occurrences except for localization [1] |
| `detail` | string | Occurrence-specific explanation; should help the client correct the problem [1] |
| `instance` | URI reference | Identifies this specific problem occurrence [1] |

Key normative statements from the specification [1]:

- "Consumers MUST use the 'type' URI (after resolution, if necessary) as the
  problem type's primary identifier."
- "The 'status' member, if present, is only advisory; it conveys the HTTP status
  code used for the convenience of the consumer."
- Generators MUST match the status member to the actual HTTP response status code.

## about:blank Default

When `type` is absent or set to `about:blank` [1]:

- The problem has no additional semantics beyond the HTTP status code
- `title` SHOULD match the standard HTTP status phrase for that code
- `about:blank` is formally registered in the IANA HTTP Problem Types registry [2]

## Media Types

| Format | Content Type | Namespace |
|--------|-------------|-----------|
| JSON | `application/problem+json` | N/A [1] |
| XML | `application/problem+xml` | `urn:ietf:rfc:7807` [1] |

The XML namespace retains the RFC 7807 URN for backward compatibility [22].

## Extension Members

Problem type definitions MAY add custom members [1]:

- Clients MUST ignore extensions they don't recognize [1]
- Names SHOULD start with a letter (ALPHA) [1]
- Names SHOULD use ALPHA, DIGIT, and underscore characters only [1]
- Names SHOULD be three characters or longer [1]
- These conventions ensure serialization compatibility with formats beyond JSON [1]

## JSON Schema (Appendix A)

RFC 9457 provides a non-normative JSON Schema using draft/2020-12/schema [1]:

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "type": { "type": "string", "format": "uri-reference" },
    "title": { "type": "string" },
    "status": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 100, "maximum": 599 },
    "detail": { "type": "string" },
    "instance": { "type": "string", "format": "uri-reference" }
  }
}
```

If there is disagreement between the schema and the specification text, the
specification text prevails [1].

## Security Considerations (Section 5)

- "When defining a new problem type, the information included must be carefully
  vetted. Likewise, when actually generating a problem, the details given must
  also be scrutinized." [1]
- Problem details are NOT debugging tools for implementation internals [1]
- Risks: exposing stack traces, leaking server information, status member/HTTP
  code disagreement [1]

## Defining New Problem Types

Required documentation [1]:

1. A type URI (http or https scheme preferred)
2. A descriptive title
3. Appropriate HTTP status code(s)

Optional: Retry-After header specification, HTML documentation at the type URI,
additional extension members using typed links [1].

## IANA Considerations

- Updated media type registrations for problem+json and problem+xml [1]
- Established new "HTTP Problem Types" registry [1] [2]
- Registration policy: "Specification Required" (RFC 8126 Section 4.6) [2]
- Designated experts: Mark Nottingham, Sanjay Dalal [2]
- Registrations MAY use prefix `https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#`
  though URIs may not be resolvable [2]
- Vendor-specific, application-specific, and deployment-specific values cannot
  be registered [2]

### Registered Problem Types (as of 2024-02-12)

| Type URI | Title | HTTP Status | Reference |
|----------|-------|-------------|-----------|
| about:blank | See HTTP Status Code | N/A | RFC 9457 [1] |
| https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#date | Date Not Acceptable | 400 | RFC 9458 [2] |
| https://iana.org/assignments/http-problem-types#ohttp-key | Oblivious HTTP key configuration not acceptable | 400 | RFC 9458 [2] |

## Changes from RFC 7807

RFC 9457 obsoletes RFC 7807 and is backward compatible [1] [17]:

| Change | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| IANA Problem Types Registry | New registry for standardized problem types [1] [2] |
| Multiple problems | Clearer guidance; HTTP 207 Multi-Status now discouraged [17] |
| Rejected Problem Header | Early draft proposed a Problem HTTP header; rejected due to protocol inconsistencies [17] |
| Type URI guidance | Stronger recommendation for absolute URIs over relative [1] [17] |
| Extension-to-type association | Clearer documentation that extensions are namespaced by problem type [1] [9] |
| JSON Pointer integration | Explicit reference to RFC 6901 for validation error location [1] [27] |

## Gaps and Limitations

- The IANA registry contains only 3 entries as of 2024-02-12, suggesting limited
  adoption of centralized type registration [2]
- W3C I18N working group identified gaps in multilingual support and text
  direction metadata (discovery agent finding, not independently verified)
- No standard mechanism for discovering available extension members for a given
  problem type
